en: *Cheng weishi lun liaoyi deng*, Scroll Three. Treatise Two.
Composed by the Bhikṣu Huizhao of Dayun Temple in Zizhou.
Regarding the treatise, there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned, as fully explained in the commentary (*shu*). However, according to the *Vibhāṣā*...
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, fascicle 38, states:
"As the Dārṣṭāntikas [hold], all conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are subsumed under the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra-skandha*)."
In his youth, he adhered to the Mahāyāna;
he was, in fact, the original teacher of the Sautrāntika school.
However, his position that [external objects] exist apart from consciousness will be refuted separately in the following section.
The Vibhajyavādins state that these characteristics are all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Dharmaguptakas state that three of the three characteristics are conditioned, while the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is unconditioned.
Since those who establish [this] as unconditioned are not the ones being refuted here, [the objection does not apply].
In the middle section below, the critique begins with the "non-correspondence" (asaṃprayoga) [view].
Although these [positions] establish conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) as being existent, they are not inconsistent [with our own position];

for in the treatise, the introduction and conclusion merely refute non-correspondence. Some say that since others have already refuted them, they need not be refuted here; however, we maintain that this is not so.
It is not that what was previously refuted by others is not now being refuted here;
rather, since the Sautrāntikas who maintain the doctrine of dissociation have already been refuted,
they are now being refuted once again.
Alternatively, although it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it functions as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Now, the meaning of its being a defining characteristic is refuted;
below, the meaning of its being unconditioned is refuted.

Refuting both positions is logically consistent with reason. As the Śramaṇa Saṃkhyātantra proclaims: "The essence of the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) is itself material;
likewise, even up to the essence of the arising, aging, abiding, and impermanence of mental phenomena (*vijñāna-dharma*), that essence is itself mental."
From here on, the refutation follows the general pattern rather than being specific to each case;
otherwise, since the essence of matter and mind would be identical to matter and mind themselves, there would be the fallacy of circularity.
The Sautrāntika masters establish their position based on the *Vibhāṣā*.
The Mahāyāna school likewise establishes four phases within a single period.
The Sarvāstivāda masters say that these are exclusively the phases of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous character).
It is not a characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
This means that the four characteristics of a single lifetime function as the defining characteristics only for the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*).
These are not the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), because every conditioned phenomenon possesses the four characteristics at every single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Thus,
the Sarvāstivādins do not admit that the four characteristics of a single duration (*eka-kāla*) are established based on the sūtras.
According to the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this is not precluded,
as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 38, provides numerous alternative explanations.
The meanings of other categories are elucidated as they appear in various treatises.
Regarding the statement that "the fact that the word is not the sixth case-ending expresses a distinct entity," the opponent establishes the following formal inference (*prayoga*):
"The word 'conditioned characteristic'..."
It must necessarily have a distinct substantial entity,
because there is a genitive case-ending [in the expression "the robe of Devadatta"],
just as in the case of Devadatta’s robe and so forth. Based on this reasoning, there are three fallacies within the [opponent's] argument.
Within this school, there is the fallacy of contradicting inference (*anumāna-viruddha-doṣa*).

The objection states: "Regarding the statement that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) have characteristics, it is not the case that they definitely possess separate intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)."
Because there is a sixth case ending [denoting possession],
as in the case of "the solidity of earth" and so forth;
the thesis does not state that there is definitely no separate entity.
However, because there is indeed something distinct from that [probandum],
there is no fallacy of the inconclusive (anaikāntika). Second, that proof possesses the fallacy of the inconclusive.
This can be understood according to the text.
Thirdly, there is also the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property to be proven (*dharma*).
This means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not merely establish a separate substantial entity.
This demonstrates that [the mark] is distinct from the characterized object.
Yet, could it be that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are the characterizing marks? If so, then things such as clothing are not conditioned characterizing marks.
Therefore, a contradiction is established;
apart from these four characteristics,
there is no further similar example (sapakṣa).
All others are not characteristics of the conditioned;
they thus constitute distinct phenomena.
This is expressed by the sixth case-ending.
Because they function differently.
This is as established in the *Nyāyapraveśa*, which posits that categories such as substance, quality, and action are not real entities;
for if a treatise were to claim that the characteristics of conditioned phenomena are different from their essential substratum (*svabhāva*), [it would contradict this principle].
The Pramāṇa states:
"Your unconditioned characteristic (asaṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) should exist separately from its substance (dravya)."
This is because it is spoken of as having characteristics,
just like the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). However, there is an interpretation which states:
It is said that this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to others;
for the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is predicated of heterogeneous instances (vipakṣa), such as solidity and so forth.
This is the fallacy of uncertainty.
This too is not a fault,
because it resides within the thesis itself.
By means of the statement "it is admitted," one generally challenges [the opponent] so that they cannot maintain this specific [position].
Furthermore, it says: "You commit the fault of self-contradiction. The Ximing [commentary] on the Pramāṇa states:
The essence of the characteristic of the unconditioned must be distinct from that which is characterized,
because it is subsumed under one of the categories within the unconditioned.
Regarding the characteristic of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), there is an interpretation which states:
this logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*),
because it is subsumed under one of the categories within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That the characterized exists while the characterizer does not is also not the case;
for a conditioned characterizer is itself conditioned,
and an unconditioned characterizer is likewise unconditioned.
Is it not the case that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) functions as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
Regarding this, the *Yāojí* (Essential Compendium) follows this [text] and states: "There is an interpretation that [the unconditioned] is superior."
Furthermore, it refutes the opponent's statement:
"The essence of your conditioned characteristics is not different from the characterized object."

Alternatively, there should be no distinct real characteristic (lakṣaṇa) as a characteristic, because it would be subsumed under one or another of the unconditioned characteristics (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
As stated in the *Yāo jí* (Essential Collection): [text follows].
Some say that this explanation serves merely as a formal proof (*pramāṇa*).
This proof, however, commits the fallacy of contradicting a specific attribute of the subject (*dharmin*) within the reason (*hetu*).
The proof states:
The essence of the characteristics of the conditioned should not be a non-associated [conditioned factor] that is merely nominal,
because it would be subsumed under one of the unconditioned [factors].

To say that, like the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this [argument] should not be established as a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) because it merely refutes by means of reasoning is an irrational statement.
Why is this? Because by establishing the thesis that the nature of your conditioned characteristics exists,
you immediately refute their inference according to their own school's tenets.
Since he does not establish his own position,
how could he contradict the proponent’s method of formal argumentation?
Furthermore, the provisional is not different from its characteristic;
the real is not different from its characteristic;
they exist separately as realities.
It does not exist as a distinct reality,
because it is a differentiation; however, this is established by way of contradiction [with the opponent's position].
This would then be a distinction of a "dharma that exists," and the word "exists" (sat) should be omitted.
If it were made a distinction of a dharma that exists...
Because of this distinction. Furthermore,
even if that were the case, their established counter-evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa) would likewise incur this fault,
because it is not substantially concomitant (asambaddha).
It is not that they are substantially existent dissociated [factors];
this is the intended meaning of the distinction.
To establish them as substantially existent dissociated factors, one sets forth the formal argument (*pramāṇa*).
Now, regarding the contradiction with valid cognition concerning the distinction between conditioned phenomena and their existence:
if you claim that the characteristic of being conditioned is truly existent,
it must not be non-associated with what is truly existent.
Because it is subsumed under either the conditioned or the unconditioned,
just like the characteristics of the unconditioned,
it cannot be established as a contradiction between a phenomenon and its differentiation.
This demonstrates that their establishment of "distinctness" (anyatva) as a separate characteristic (lakṣaṇa) external to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta)—
like the "cloth of Yājña"— is a case of a counter-balanced reason (pratibādhaka-sama) that contradicts the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the subject (dharmin).
Furthermore, there are contradictions regarding the specific characteristics of phenomena and the fallacy of counter-balanced reasons (*pratibhāga*). Moreover, the faults are as previously stated.
For this reason, some say that there is an interpretation free from error.
Treatise:
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the characteristics such as arising are co-existent in substance," the original text says:
First, he refutes the ancient masters' view that the functions of the characteristics occur sequentially.

Furthermore, below the section on "abiding, change, and cessation," he refutes the new Sautrāntika-Sarvāstivādins' view that the three characteristics function simultaneously. The Ximing commentary states:
It encompasses both the new and the old [traditions].
Some take the former as correct; the *Yaoji* states that taking Ximing as correct is right.
Regarding the textual meaning of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are two interpretations.
The first states that the times of their activity differ;
this refers to the sequence of the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, it says:
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that aging has its activity precisely at the time of cessation;
therefore, it occurs simultaneously [with cessation]. Now, I say this is not so.
As previously cited from the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 39, it says:
This demonstrates that a single moment possesses three characteristics.
Question: If this is so, then a single dharma would also possess arising, aging, and cessation. Answer:
There is no contradiction, because their functional activities occur at different times.
That is to say, when a phenomenon arises, "arising" has its functional activity;
when it ceases, "aging" and "cessation" then have their functional activities.
Although their substance is simultaneous, their functions occur in temporal succession.
This intention is precisely to answer that the functions of the three characteristics all possess a sequence of before and after;
it does not separately state that cessation and aging are simultaneous.
The treatise says this is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and revealing the correct meaning.
If, as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain, the three characteristics exist within a single moment,
then a single dharma would simultaneously be arising, aging, and ceasing; however,
such a principle is impossible.
Because they are mutually contradictory,
one should explain that the initial arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called "birth" (*jāti*),
and their subsequent exhaustion is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
The middle stage of decline is called "aging.
To refute that [notion] and demonstrate that a single moment possesses the three characteristics, it is asked: "If this is so..."
Then it would follow that a single dharma would simultaneously undergo arising, aging, and cessation.
Answer: Because the times of their activity differ, there is no contradiction. ...
[and so on] ... until it says:
Although the essence [of phenomena] exists simultaneously, their functions occur sequentially;
since the completion of a single phenomenon's process of arising and ceasing constitutes one *kṣaṇa*,
there is no logical error.
The stages of arising and ceasing do not occupy a single moment;
however, because a single moment possesses all three natures, it is said that the three characteristics exist within one and the same moment. (End of the cited treatise.)
Regarding the statement that "aging has its function precisely at the time of cessation":
this is because aging, as a phenomenon of decay, becomes manifest only when it ceases;
thus, it is said that aging has its function precisely at the time of cessation.
Therefore, the following provides a summary:
although their essence (tattva) exists simultaneously, their functions (vṛtti) occur sequentially;
furthermore, it is not stated that abiding (sthiti) and cessation (nirodha) are simultaneous.
Therefore, one should know that the sequential application of the ancient masters' views ought not to be divided into two separate doctrines,
as there is no distinction in the text. Furthermore, in the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the Sarvāstivāda is refuted.
Furthermore, since the three functions— stability and so forth— are all present simultaneously,
it would follow that within a single moment of a single dharma-substance,
there must be stability, decay, and destruction occurring at once.
When the characteristic of duration causes this dharma to abide,
is it called "abiding" (sthiti) or is it called "alteration" (anyathātva)?
This would result in the destruction of the [concept of] "name.
Furthermore, the various explanations that the functions of abiding and so forth do not occur simultaneously would contradict the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*).
Since he himself asserts that the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and functions (kāritra) occur sequentially,
he simultaneously challenges the ancient Sarvāstivādins; thus,
there is a parallel difficulty in challenging the new Sarvāstivādins regarding the sequential nature of characteristics and functions.
This is also consistent with the original text; therefore, it relies on the correct treatise.
Regarding the point that "the causes and conditions upon which [a result] depends should not be inherently existent," the Commentary answers this external objection by stating:
"Although phenomena that are empty and insubstantial may currently possess seeds..."
If there are no external conditions, [the effect] cannot arise because it is weak and deficient.
How can your "real dharmas" (bhūta-dharma) serve as a valid analogy? The *Yaoji* says:

This explanation does not fully capture the underlying principle. We now maintain that although the substance of the seeds is eternal, the conditions upon which they depend are originally non-existent and now come into being;
thus, their successive arising is infinite.
Because it is not constantly present,
it is not a permanent birth.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 51, states:
Although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have their own respective causes for arising,
they must nonetheless depend upon conditions (*pratyaya*) in order to grow and develop.
Therefore, this treatise states:
Regarding the statement that "it differs from the non-Buddhists because it does not arise all at once since its object is never non-existent":
this current explanation is no different from the original position, as it still depends on external conditions;
these external conditions are, moreover, distinct from the immediate seed itself.
If external conditions have not yet converged, [the effect] cannot arise.
Since these conditions are not constantly present, they are simply the aforementioned causes;
why labor to state them separately? Now, let us further raise an objection.
Just as I [hold that] external conditions exist outside of consciousness,
yet [cognition] does not arise when they are incomplete or not simultaneous;
so too in the Mahāyāna, it is solely one's own mind.
It does not depend on external phenomena outside of consciousness for these to arise suddenly. Answer: The immediate object of perception is solely one's own consciousness;
because it cannot perceive the external, it is called "Mind-Only.
This does not mean that other sentient beings, acting as dominant conditions, do not exist.
Furthermore, that which is not present does not arise instantaneously.
Moreover, the opponent offers this defense:
"Although your seeds exist in the present..."
That which is empty and insubstantial depends on adventitious conditions;
that which is the substantial essence of self and dharmas likewise depends on real external conditions.
If that were so, then the very notion of the two types of arising would be rendered useless.
As for the argument in the treatise that "the characterized object (lakṣya) exists eternally, yet it is conjoined with arising and so forth":

Question: What is the difference between this refutation and the previous reasoning? Answer: Previously, it was refuted by taking as an example the fact that the opponent’s school does not establish a separate defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) apart from the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), thereby preventing them from establishing one separately for the conditioned (saṃskṛta).
In the present case, the refutation proceeds differently.
Now, since the conditioned entity is said to be eternally existent and thus associated with arising and so forth,
by analogy, the unconditioned entity is likewise eternally existent.
Because they should be combined with "arising" (*utpāda*) and so forth, the two texts differ.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* says:
In that case, "being other than the former" is not established;
for to be other than the former is not to be a single dharma.
If it were the dharma that is being made other...
If that which was previously abiding is what is currently abiding,
the meaning of "difference" is not established;
for that which previously abided is not a separate dharma.
That is not a single dharma.
[The] treatise asks:
what fault is there in indicating that this is the characteristic of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) hereafter?
The original commentary states:
"That is to say, when a present phenomenon no longer exists at a later time,
it is termed 'cessation'."
To speak metaphorically of the past:
the essence of the past does not truly exist, for it is not that world. The Ximing commentary states:
"The characteristic of cessation is provisional."
It is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha);
it is conventionally dependent upon reality,
yet substantially exists in the past.
If one were to say that the present should depend on a different time,
this refers to the characteristic of cessation (nirodha-lakṣaṇa). The treatise states that the last [characteristic] is past because it is non-existent.
If it is argued that they depend on the present,
and that there is a mutual dependence between different time periods,
he offers his own explanation for this objection:
If one relies on the past, there would be no basis [for cognition].
The answer is: it is like the case in inference where a non-existent entity is established;
in that instance, the reason (*hetu*) is also established by relying on what is non-existent.
It is not the case that every finite cause must have a basis;
the characteristic of cessation is non-existent.
What fault is there in its having no basis?
Some interpret the former primary commentary as being correct;
for although the latter explanation lacks a mutual dependence between different time periods,
it does possess a mutual manifestation between different time periods.

Furthermore, that which has already ceased is non-existent, because it is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*), just like the hair of a tortoise and so forth. The *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) intends to take the latter explanation as correct. The *Fifty-two* [Treatise] states:
"It is based on the state of having perished after arising."
It establishes impermanence.
Furthermore, the forty-sixth [section] states:
"Based on the 'constituent of existence' (bhavāṅga), one type of conditioned characteristic is established."
Based on the absence of parts, one establishes a single characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, this treatise states:
"That which has no time is called cessation."
Regarding the temporal states explained herein:
it is not possible to speak of states without time,
nor is it the case that there is time without states.
From this, it may be inferred accordingly that the state of having already ceased is established as the past, and so forth. Now, I say:
The explanation provided in this commentary is correct.
Why? For instance, regarding the establishment of the *Lokadhātu* (World System): the world is established based upon the *dharmas*.
Although one speaks of the past and the future,
the past and the future have no intrinsic nature;
they still depend upon the present dharma.
The past, future, and present times are established in dependence [on one another].
The characteristic of cessation exists in the past;
since the past is conventionally designated in reliance upon the present dharma.
The principle of the characteristic of cessation actually depends upon the present;
therefore, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The various stages are provisionally established upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)."
Alternatively, it is an image of a state within the mind.
The time referred to here pertains to all three periods,
yet the designation of the "three" is applied only to the present.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, fascicle 2, states:
"Time" refers to the provisional designation of "time" based upon the continuous flow and circulation of cause and effect. Furthermore, the third [fascicle] states:
"The past and future are provisionally designated in dependence upon the present."
Therefore, the future is conventionally established based on what is to be attained, and the past is conventionally established based on what has been attained. Furthermore, this treatise states:
"This indicates that there is nothing subsequent"; and it also states: "Cessation indicates that after a functional entity (dharma), there is non-existence."

If one does not rely on the observation of the present life to understand the meaning of "having existed," but instead merely grasps at the non-existence of phenomena to establish a past time and the characteristic of cessation;
As the treatise states: "That which lacks time is called 'extinction.
The past is truly non-existent;
however, both the characteristic of extinction and the temporal period are real."
How can it be called a "nominal designation" (prajñapti)?
And how can it be said that this expresses "non-existence after"?
It should rather be said that it expresses that the preceding phenomenon has already ceased to exist.
Furthermore, this contradicts the third chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which establishes the three time periods based on the present;
for that [text] applies to all phenomena by way of their past and future causes and effects.
Moreover, the first chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Mental non-associated factors cannot be designated as being either identical to or different from mental states.
Since the characteristic of cessation cannot be established based on the past,
its temporal and substantial nature is entirely incompatible with that of present phenomena.
How can it not be designated as something distinct?
Furthermore, if it were merely non-existence,
why does [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] state in the fifty-second [fascicle]:
Question: As the Blessed One has said, "There are past formations," and so forth, up to:
"What is the underlying intention (saṃdhi) of this?"
Answer: Past formations exist because they have already yielded their fruit;
future formations exist because they encompass their causes.
Otherwise, since the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the past and future would be non-existent, [the system would fail].
How can it be said that causes are subsumed by their fruits? Therefore,
based on the fact that causes subsume their fruits within the present life,
one metaphorically designates them as "past" or "future."
Furthermore, how can it be said that one contemplates the arising and ceasing within the aggregates?
Cessation depends upon the past,
yet the past is non-existent.
There are no phenomena that are not aggregates.

Question: Since the past is provisionally established in dependence upon the present, how can it be said that there is no time called "extinction"? Furthermore, [the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*] states in section 46:
Past formations have already arisen and already ceased;
regarding those formations, no cause can be found,
nor do they possess intrinsic nature.
It is further said:
"One correctly contemplates that this very momentary arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is itself destruction by its own nature."
Answer: One observes that within the present dharma there is a retribution for preceding conditions;
these causes are conventionally designated as "past," and they are termed "already arisen" and "having their intrinsic nature destroyed."
It is not that the present dharma is absent while only the past is taught;
therefore, the *Fifty-two* [Scrolls] states:

"If the continuity of seeds that have already yielded their fruit is called the 'past realm' (*atīta-dhātu*). Since it refers to the continuity of seeds as the "past realm," [the distinction between the two is established].
It clarifies that the essence of the seed is not something already extinguished. Question: How can that which has not yet been extinguished in the present dharma be established as "extinguished"?
Furthermore, how could all manifest activities (pravṛtti) lack the characteristic of extinction? Answer: For now, this is based on the seeds to reveal the past realm.
The reflection is manifested in the present;
just as when it has not yet yielded its fruit,
the continuity of the seed is termed the "present realm."
It is not only seeds that are uniquely termed "present," for the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu) pertain to all three time periods; alternatively,
one may simply speak of "seeds."
The element (*dhātu*) is so named because it is a cause that is constantly continuous;
alternatively, even its actual manifestation may be called a "seed" (*bīja*),
because it is capable of producing a fruit.
As stated in the eighth assembly regarding the "ten causes and two causes" and the "seeds," both actual seeds and manifest phenomena possess the characteristic of cessation.
This is because one observes that manifest phenomena have the function of repaying prior conditions.
It is conventionally designated as such because it has already ceased;
thus, the characteristic of cessation is said to exist in the past,
since the dharma has already passed away.
The characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is then manifested. In reality, because that which is presently existing will necessarily cease,
it is also termed "cessation."

This is just as the treatise expresses it: there is no such thing as a conventionally designated characteristic of cessation that exists apart from the cessation of suffering and pleasure, which is like the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*);
yet, it is said that pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*) is also called the suffering of change.
This means that because it is suffering at the time of its destruction,
the same applies to the present life as well;
and because it must necessarily cease, it is called "past."
Because it is manifested at this time,
because it differs from other schools, and because it is categorized according to the [three] periods;
thus, the fifty-second [fascicle] states:
For what reason does the Blessed One speak of only three types:
first, arising;
second, cessation?
Third, the difference in abiding.
Answer: Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are manifested by the three time periods;
they arise from the future, having previously been non-existent.
Therefore, the Blessed One, by means of the future world,
speaks of "arising" as a conditioned characteristic of conditioned phenomena,
and so on, up to [the past world].
Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), cessation is said to be a characteristic of the conditioned.
Phenomena in the present state are manifested by two characteristics, namely:
duration (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*).
Since they exist as the two characteristics of abiding and change in the present,
it is clear that arising occurs in the future and cessation exists in the past.
According to the conventional meaning, they are divided [into three times]; however, based on their actual status as provisional designations, they can be applied to all three times.
Otherwise, the four characteristics would not be universal to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
If that which is present and that which is future were not subject to cessation, they would not be impermanent.
The fifty-second [fascicle] states:
"Furthermore, there are also many varieties of the distinctions of impermanence."

That is to say: the impermanence of disintegration, the impermanence of arising, the impermanence of transformation, the impermanence of dissolution, the impermanence of what is yet to come, and the impermanence of present falling away.
If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), having arisen, immediately perish, this is called the impermanence of destruction (*bhaṅga-anityatā*).
That which was originally non-existent now comes into being is called the impermanence of arising (*utpāda-anityatā*).
The arising of conditioned phenomena with different characteristics is called the impermanence of transformation (*anyathātva-anityatā*).
The disintegration and loss [of conditioned phenomena] is called "dissolution impermanence.

These four types of impermanence, when existing in the future time, are called "future existence impermanence. When they are actually present before one, [they are called "present occurrence impermanence"].
It is said that they "manifestly fall into impermanence"; by analogy with this, one should know that they also pertain to the three time periods (*adhvan*).

This is because [the text] provides a detailed explanation of the distinctions among the four preceding characteristics. Furthermore, it explains that they exist only in the present, as there would otherwise be the fault of having no distinction between the past and the future.
Because the three [time periods] are established based on the present,
although they actually depend on the present,
their meaning extends throughout the three time periods.
There is no fault of non-pervasiveness.

yet they do not know it to be unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) with respect to non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
To cognize the substance of a phenomenon but not its meaning means to know that this phenomenon does not arise due to the absence of conditions,
and that the substance of the phenomenon has ceased and no longer exists.
Not knowing that this is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is called "not understanding the meaning. According to this treatise, it may also be said to be twofold:
first, that which arises through the transformation of consciousness; second, that which does not arise through the transformation of consciousness.
Because the provisional and the real are distinct;
that which depends on the transformation of consciousness is not truly [existent], as it appears as something other than reality.
Some establish three [categories],
following the Hīnayāna; furthermore,
this is for the sake of both the mundane and the supramundane.
Space is not a result of analytical discernment, because it is not free from bondage.
Cessation through analytical discernment is supramundane. Some establish four [types of cessation].
The *Tattvasaṃgraha* and the *Pañcaskandhaka-prakaraṇa* were composed to distinguish between the conventional and the ultimate regarding both the doctrines of other schools and our own tenets. Space,
analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation are established in common with others.
Suchness (tathatā) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are of intrinsic nature;
the first three are provisional, while the last one is real. Therefore, this treatise establishes six [categories].
Based on analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), two types are distinguished according to the distinction between the obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and concentration (*samādhi*):
the immovable cessation (*āniñjya-nirodha*) and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
Because it obstructs meditative concentration,
it is difficult to know within concentration;
furthermore, it is divided into two types.
Or it is due to the determinate or the indeterminate,
the immovable, perception and feeling,
their permanent abandonment, and analytical cessation.

This is a temporary suppression rather than a definitive discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā*). Because the subject and its support are distinct, *tathatā* (suchness) is established; alternatively, it is distinguished as being either provisional or substantial.
In the Abhidharma, eight categories are established;
within the context of suchness (*tathatā*), they are divided into three by way of their verbal designation:
namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.
This treatise establishes only one [category] based on its essential meaning;
however, if one relies on the conventional designations of linguistic expression, there is no fault in establishing even many more.
There are three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) distinguished by their different categories.
The first is established based on suchness (*tathatā*);
it is truly unconditioned.
The second [type] is established based on consciousness;
it resembles the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in some respects, while in other respects its substance is actually conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Third, it is established by way of a distinct meaning:
that is to say, all untainted phenomena (anāsrava) are called "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) because they are not produced by afflictions (kleśa).
Because they arise from causes and conditions, they are subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The first is not a cause or condition for defilement or purification;
the subsequent ones may be both.
Alternatively, it is not defiled,
because the mind of the three natures can all undergo transformation; therefore,
it is subsequently not defiled.
However, if one analyzes its essential nature,
it is indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
because it arises from causes. This concludes the brief question and answer.

For what reason is the true suchness (tathatā) manifested by the abandonment of the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa) called "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)? [And] as for the abandonment of the obstructions to the knowable (jñeyāvaraṇa)...
It is not called "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), but is simply called "cessation" (nirodha). Answer: Because it is not definitive.
As stated in the tenth [chapter] below:
"The two types, such as the immovable [attainments], are cessations through temporary suppression."
That which is comprised by non-analytical cessation is [the cessation] not through deliberation; that which is ultimate cessation is comprised by analytical cessation.
This is the same as in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. Question: The same applies to afflictions (*kleśa*).

What is meant by "discrimination" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and what is "non-discrimination" (*apratisaṃkhyā*)? Answer: Afflictions are easily [recognized] and are commonly accepted as being equivalent to discrimination.
Because that which is known is difficult to realize and not common [to all], it is designated merely as "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Alternatively, they are mutually implied by their shadows,
or the names are established according to their respective applications.

One cannot be held equally accountable for the distinctions between *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation). [The former] is attained according to deliberation; [the latter] is attained in states where there is no arising [of defilements].

Why is it not the same for the *āniñjya-saṃskāra* (imperturbable formations) regarding perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*)? Answer: This statement is made on the basis of ultimate abandonment.
The two [aspects] are also established even in the absence of the non-obstructive portion;
this is based on the manifest [aspect], understood as being equal,
or alternatively, it refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the two meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Because those two concentrations have not yet been attained in the other stages,
the attainment of knowledge and concentration are not simultaneous.
This is because one necessarily attains knowledge upon abandoning whichever afflictions are severed.

If the feelings of suffering and pleasure, as well as perception and feeling, have not yet been extinguished, it is because one has not yet attained that meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Question: Defilements do not obstruct concentration;
this applies only to the category of the knowable (*jñeya*).
Afflictions also obstruct meditative concentration;
thus, they should be said to pertain to both types of obstructions. Answer: In reality, both indeed obstruct concentration, but this is stated according to what is predominant.
Because one experiences inferior meditative absorption through the ripening of karma (*vipāka-vedanā*),
it obstructs superior absorption, which is superior to other defiled states; thus,
this refers specifically to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Without specifying [the distinction between] afflictions, [the question is asked: To which category do the transformations of consciousness into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as the objective-image portions (*nimittabhāga*) arising from conditions directed toward the unconditioned, belong?
Answer: They are subsumed under the aspect (*nimitta*) and follow along with the vision (*darśana*).
These are subsumed within the four aggregates (*skandha*).
They are explained separately as "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "characteristic" (*nimitta*); they are included within the same category of phenomena (*dharmasabhāga*).
Alternatively, according to the treatise, there are two types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*): first, those that exist as transformations of consciousness;
although they are substantially conditioned, they are nonetheless subsumed under the category of the unconditioned.
Because the characteristics follow the substance and the provisional follows the real,
there are further questions and answers as extensively analyzed elsewhere.
These two forms of attachment to dharmas are subtle and therefore difficult to sever.
The *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium) summarizes three interpretations.
The first states that the six or seven types of dharma-grasping have existed from beginningless time and arise with the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) from the same seeds.
Apart from the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), there is no separate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). That [position] is correct;
it is said that this grasping at phenomena consists of exactly one hundred and twenty-eight types.
It is identical with the afflictions; however, we now say this is not so.
From beginningless time, one has clung to phenomena as existing, and thus clung to them as a self.
It may be as you have said.
Although those who hold views such as the view of nirvāṇa maintain that phenomena exist,
they do not maintain them to be a self.
Is this not an attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)? Since these are attachments to phenomena,
how could they ever be concomitant with an attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*)?
Furthermore, since the self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) of a small Arhat has already been severed,
how could they not give rise to clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*)? If clinging to phenomena were to arise...
Is it permitted that seeds are perfumed? If they are not perfumed,
what deficiency prevents [the result]?
If you allow for the perfuming of seeds,
why would they not produce manifest phenomena? Since these do indeed produce manifest phenomena, [the seeds must exist].
Is it not the case that [the innate clinging to a self] always shares the same seed as the clinging to a self?

Although it is said that there are one hundred and twenty-eight categories, it is not stated that each is of the same seed as its respective affliction. Question: Regarding the abandonment of the innate clinging to phenomena associated with the sixth consciousness—
Question: Are there gradual, sudden, sequential, or non-sequential [methods of abandonment]? Answer: There is only gradual abandonment in sequence, not by skipping stages.
This is because there is no sudden attainment of the fruits [of the path] nor skipping over the stages (*bhūmi*). If that is so, why do the two vehicles abandon the obstacles of afflictions?
First subduing and later transcending;
the Bodhisattva abandons the objects of knowledge.
Later transcending and also first subduing. Answer: It is easy for the followers of the Two Vehicles to attain their fruits.
First subduing and later transcending;
the realization of the stages in the Mahāyāna is difficult.
There can be no transcendence where there is nothing to be subdued. Question: It is difficult to attain the fruit in the Mahāyāna.
Only the sequential [births] are mentioned, not the skipping.
Regarding "feeding the tiger" and "covering the mud," how can one speak of skipping kalpas? Answer: In the Mahāyāna, there is no skipping of stages (bhūmi).
According to this, it does not mention "leaping over" [kalpas].
Since birth is brought about by diligence,
what prevents one from attaining the leaping over of kalpas?
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that "the function of being an object-condition must depend upon a substantially existent entity," a question is raised:
if a phenomenon lacking an entity has no status as an object-condition, [how can this be so?]
Regarding that which possesses an object of perception (*sālambana*):
why is the first [case] mentioned first?
Because it is not the state in which atoms (*paramāṇu*) are in mutual conjunction.

[Question: Can it serve as an object-condition (*ālambana*) for each of the five consciousnesses? [Answer: Because the five consciousnesses cannot take subtle objects as their conditions, it is said that [the mental image] is not an object-condition for them.

However, it does not obstruct the sixth consciousness from taking it as an object-condition by means of a non-transformed aspect (*nirākāra*). [Question: If that is so, why is it called the "contemplation of the object-condition"?

Question: It is said that the atom (*paramāṇu*) may serve as a condition for the five consciousnesses, but not as an object-condition (*ālambana*). Answer: This response refutes the status of the object-condition;

even if one were to grant the sense of it being a condition, no substantial entity can function as a condition in relation to the six consciousnesses. Question: Do not both provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) and non-existents fail to function as conditions?
In the Mahāyāna, the sixth [consciousness] takes things such as rabbit horns as its objects.
Since these objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) are provisional, can they still function as objects of cognition?
If you admit that it constitutes a condition,
why do you refute others? If it does not constitute a condition, [why do you refute them?]

Is it not the case that there are no objects of direct perception? Answer: The Hīnayāna schools and others maintain that dharmas external to consciousness—whether provisional or real—do not exist at all, and thus they do not constitute objects of direct perception.
Therefore, it was refuted previously.
That which is the object-condition (*ālambana*) in the Mahāyāna is not separate from consciousness,
as this excludes the parikalpita (imagined nature).
All are designated as both name and reality,
and they constitute the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Treatise.
Regarding the point that "it is not an object of cognition because it is comprised within another aggregate," there may be no similar example for this,
since the five or seven types of objects of cognition are not all-pervasive.

It is said that [the sixth consciousness] is not an object of perception (*anālambana*). Since the sixth [consciousness] universally perceives the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), why is it not an object of perception?
Answer: This is stated according to the perspective of specific perception (*pṛthak-ālambana*).

Because it is commonly accepted by both [parties]. Question: Since it is commonly accepted that the Buddha’s wisdom universally takes both self and others as its objects, why is it not an object of cognition?
Answer: Because it is explained in terms of causes.
Furthermore, it is because it is accepted by the other party that the Buddha’s mind is not able to universally take all things as its objects at all times.
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "the present collection,
etc.," the refutation of the opponent's position may be understood by following the text.
However, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"What is the knowledge of others' minds?
It knows its object as it is not."
"Just as the mind that knows itself does not know [itself] as it is in the realm of a Buddha":
this passage contains the interrogation, the explanation, the application, and the response.
The first two phrases constitute an external inquiry.
This is because, in the previous response, it was stated that apart from the Buddha,
although others know the minds of others...
However, it is not as it truly is;
taking another as its object,
the appearing aspect (nimitta-bhāga) resembles it only slightly.
It cannot describe reality;
it differs from the essential nature.
Because it is not according to reality, [the opponent] now raises an objection.
Regarding the question of how the knowledge of others' minds knows its object as it truly is— just as one knows one's own mind—
the Master of the Treatise explains:
it does not grasp the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) while taking that very seeing-part as its object.
Once [the Buddha] has eliminated [all else], nothing other than the Buddha can serve as an object-condition,
because it is based on a single moment and lacks the measure of temporal succession. Furthermore,
because he knows things as they truly are, this is not a case of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
One grasps the preceding and succeeding conditions, as well as the distinct cognitions that serve as conditions;
because these also manifest as appearances, one does not know them as they truly are. Furthermore, another then says:
"How does one know that both self and other are unable to [know] as it truly is?"— the two characters "not knowing" in the fourth line of the verse constitute the Master’s response.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds, with the exception of the Buddha,
it is obscured by the grasping at phenomena (dharmagrāha),
whether in its active manifestation or as a seed.
Because this ignorance obscures both the mind and its objects, one is unable to know them.
It is precisely due to this obscuration that one does not know the ineffable realm as it is traversed by the pure wisdom of a Buddha.
First, by stating "I do not know," he provides a comprehensive answer to the preceding question and simultaneously reveals that his lack of knowledge is as it was with the Buddha;
this is the intended meaning of the treatise.
The verse states that "not knowing" refers to the combination of ignorance and non-cognition, which together are termed "ignorance" (ajñāna). This applies generally and extends to the answer as well.
The Commentary (*Shu*) says:
However, the calculation of the Venerable [Śrīlāta] and others is that the mental factors associated with a single collection of consciousness are also mutually capable of being objects of cognition.
As the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:
The Dharmaguhya school asserts this:
wisdom and the other [faculties] are able to cognize associated factors such as feeling;
this intention does not state that each is able to take itself as its own object.
They mutually take one another as objects. The *Vibhāṣā* further states:
"Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the mind and mental factors are able to cognize their coexistent [factors]."
For example, the Mahīśāsaka school asserts this:
"Wisdom is of two kinds that arise simultaneously."
First, association;
second, dissociation. One who possesses wisdom associated [with the path] understands that which is dissociated.
Regarding the statement that "non-associated wisdom knows that which is associated," the Master of the *Abhidharmakośa* explains:
"To say 'associated' means it is associated with the mental complex (*citta-kalāpa*) that arises simultaneously."
Regarding "non-associated," this refers to preceding and succeeding moments of thought,
which do not associate with a simultaneous collection of mental factors.
These two types of wisdom know one another.
At present, the meaning of the term "coexistent dharmas" (*sahabhū-dharma*) has not yet been fully clarified;
furthermore, the interpretations of the Western masters shall be examined later upon consulting the relevant texts.
Now, another explanation states:
that which is called "associated" refers to the four aggregates;
that which is "dissociated" refers to the aggregate of form.
As well as the four aggregates preceding and following [the mind],
these coexist with the four aggregates;
they do not take their own associated factors as objects.
The non-associated aggregates that arise simultaneously with the cognitive object are called "simultaneously apprehended";
the associated aggregates are known by subsequent cognitions.
The wisdom that arises before and after is itself not associated with this wisdom,
yet it is able to know the four aggregates associated with this wisdom.
The Mahāsāṃghika school asserts that knowledge which is mutually correlated with what precedes and follows knows one another;
for since knowledge and its like have the capacity to cognize as their intrinsic nature,
they are able to cognize both themselves and others.
Just as a lamp, because its intrinsic nature is to illuminate,
can illuminate both itself and others.
Treatise.
Regarding the phrase "as with true fire and so forth," the original text states:
"Within that which is dependent upon others, there exists a semblance of phenomena (dharma) but no semblance of a self (ātman)."
"Dharma" means that which serves as a norm and sustains itself;
it exists within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
"Self" (*ātman*) means a sovereign controller.
Within the dependent nature,
phenomena arise from distinct seeds;
for me, there are no distinct seeds.
That which does not obstruct is called "resembling" [the object];
it exists merely as a distinction between presence and absence.
Others for the most part do not understand this.
Various alternative interpretations have been offered;

however, these fail to capture the intended meaning when discussing the human-like nature of the "fierce one" (*mṛga*) and so forth, as well as the fact that [the cognition] takes both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
To raise such objections is to lose the core tenet of the system.
I am too weary to provide a detailed exposition.
Regarding the formal syllogisms (pramāṇa) established in the Commentary (*śāstra*), consider this example: when the sixth consciousness perceives a person named Zhang.
All other phenomena within the human body should likewise be objects of attachment through conditions;
although this inference is formulated according to the tenets of another school,
[it applies even] when the mind of one's own Mahāyāna school is in a state of meditative concentration.
Can one apprehend all phenomena as a human person? If not,
then it would not be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not apprehended.
If it is granted that there is acquisition (*prāpti*),
then the person (*pudgala*) is a conventional phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*) and lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as a common characteristic.
How does direct perception (pratyakṣa) obtain its object? Answer: The mind of direct perception obtains the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Each [cognition] is attached to its own basis and clearly knows the composite phenomena (saṃghāta-dharma) conventionally designated as a "person" (pudgala).
To form a single interpretation [of this] is not called "attaining the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This explains the burning of the mind and speech.
The opponent (the outsider) raises a counter-objection.

If your concentrated mind and the five or eight consciousnesses apprehend the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, why does it not burn the mind when perceiving fire? [Answer: The tenets of our respective systems differ.
You maintain that verbal expression apprehends the specific characteristic.
Just as when the body faculty encounters the specific characteristic of fire,
it perceives burning heat,
because fire has burning heat as its specific characteristic.
The same applies to the mind and so forth.
Since they have already attained their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), why are they not burned?
This is an objection raised by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is not the tenet of the Mahāyāna school.
According to the Mahāyāna school, the faculties are not what is burned;
yet you claim that they attain their own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Each is attained by being clearly distinguished from its own substance;
this attainment of its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) through non-discriminative penetration is not like that of the non-Buddhists.

If non-Buddhists or those of other vehicles each maintain that verbal expressions apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon, and that this is likewise the case for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*),
they raise this objection.
The Mahāyāna is not thus, and therefore it has no fault of its own.
As for the statement that "one now takes blue as the object and forms a cognition of blue," this inferential knowledge does not correspond to the preceding phenomenon.
Just as visual consciousness, when perceiving form, does not produce the conceptual understanding of "form" because it apprehends its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);

subsequently, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), arising and perceiving the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of that form, produces the conceptual understanding of "blue" and so forth. Question: As for the previous statement that although one may perceive a jar, if one does not grasp it with dogmatic adherence, it is subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). How is this?

Question: Why is the cognition of "blue" not called inference (*anumāna*)? Answer: The cognition of a jar as a single entity based on multiple factors does not accord with the actual nature of the phenomenon and is therefore subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
The cognition of "blue," however, does not depend on multiple factors and accords with the actual nature of the phenomenon.
Because it is subsumed under conceptual inference (*savikalpānumāna*). If that is so, does the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) produce a cognition of blue and so forth?
If it does not produce such a cognition, how can one perform the meditative observation of blue and so forth in the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) and *abhibhvāyatana* (mastery) exercises?

If one forms a cognition of blue and so forth, that concentrated mind should be considered an inference. Answer: Although the cognition of blue is formed as being attached to its own specific entity and does not extend to others, it is nonetheless direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The contemplation of impurity and other such practices may be understood by analogy with this.

It is asked: "How is it that conventional cognition, which functions based on common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), is said to 'function' (*vartate*) because it takes [an object] as its condition?"
If "transformation" (parāvṛtti) refers to the activity of practice and understanding,
or if it refers to being an object of cognition, then its substantial reality as a universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) would be non-existent.

Question: Upon what does cognition arise? Answer: Although the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) is superimposed upon the particular characteristic (sva-lakṣaṇa) of the underlying substance as if it were truly existent, when conventional cognition takes it as its object, it nevertheless relies upon that underlying substance by transforming it into an objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga).
Since both substance and characteristic are absent, that common characteristic lacks an essential nature.
Cognition merely takes the characteristic as its object;
it cannot apprehend or adhere to that common characteristic.
The explanation of meaning takes the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object;
it clarifies that the expression does not adhere to the object, and thus the name functions in dependence upon the common [characteristic].
Alternatively, even in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it may be termed "functioning" (*vṛtti*).

However, when such a conceptual construction arises, that universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) does not exist [as an objective reality]. If this is so, why is it said to "function based on a universal characteristic"? Answer: It functions based on the conceptualization of a universal characteristic. If this is so, what is the difference between the conceptual construction and its cognitive function (*ālambana-vṛtti*)? Answer: It is like the mind of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha-citta*); although its object is non-self (*anātman*), [the mind still functions toward it].
Yet, one clings to these through one's own emotional delusions and falsely constructs them as one’s own understanding.
It is precisely because of this false understanding that the grasping mind arises.
Thus, the Treatise says:
Regarding the phrase "arising from the conceptualization of the marks of one's own mind" (*svacittanimittavikalpa*), which refers to the grasping at a real self (*ātman*),
there are two interpretations in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
This [explanation] follows the latter interpretation.

The same applies to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Although this conventional cognition (*prajñaptijñāna*) is not a firm attachment, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) resembles that [of the former].
If that is so, then the object apprehended (*grāhya*) by the mode of activity and the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—[these are what are meant].
Since both lack intrinsic nature, how can they function as conditions? Answer:
When conventional cognition functions as a condition, the mind necessarily arises with respect to the substance and its characteristics, according to their respective requirements.
Thus, the meaning of "condition" is established.

It is not the case that the mind arises independently of an object that lacks substantial characteristics. Question: Since it has been argued that the substance of form is in reality neither blue nor yellow, when a conventional cognition (*prajñapti*) designates and conditions something as "blue," [how does this occur]?
Is it for the purpose of negation or for the purpose of affirmation? If it were merely for negation,
there would be no object of expression to serve as a condition.
How is it that real form and so forth are said to possess blue, yellow, and so on?
If there is also manifestation (vijñapti),
it then expresses the perception of blue and so forth.

How can it be said that one does not apprehend the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)? Answer: It is like the expression "form" (rūpa), which is a conventional designation (prajñapti) based upon the phenomenon;
its essence is not actually form in the same way that the word suggests.
The same applies to blue and so forth.
It merely excludes others;
the intention is to indicate this.
Thus, it is said that [the teaching] both excludes and indicates.
One does not apprehend the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) by means of the manifest (vijñapti) alone.
When the five [sense-cognitions] and the eighth [mental consciousness] encounter their objects,
they do not form conceptualizations such as "matter" or "non-matter," or "blue" or "non-blue."
Since one attains the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) by taking the characterized object as a condition through direct realization,
[one might ask: in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), where there is no sound,
upon what does conventional cognition (prajñapti-jñāna) depend to arise?
The answer has three interpretations:
first, it is spoken according to the majority;
second, it is because of the term "also" (api).
This is explained in terms of the fruit of meditative concentration.
Those who previously, while in the two lower realms, repeatedly heard of that [object] will,
due to such habitual practice, give rise to a conventional cognition as well.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* asks: "Both the signifier and the signified lack their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If both the signifier and the signified lack their own specific characteristics, they can function based on a commonality."

If it is argued that the subjective grasper (*ālambaka*) and the objective grasped (*ālambana*) are not said to be non-self-characterized (*asvalakṣaṇa*), then they should not depend on co-arising (*saha-vartana*). Answer: The conceptual cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*) that acts as the grasper is also not self-characterized;

it is called "conceptual cognition" because it possesses discrimination (*vikalpa*). Question: Why is this not explicitly stated? Answer: It is due to abbreviation (*saṃkṣepa*); by mentioning the object (*viṣaya*), the mind (*citta*) is implied.
Commentary:
"Seemingly" refers to superimposition (*samāropa*).
The original text says:
Superimposing a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) upon a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Ximing states:
For instance, when visual consciousness apprehends the blue specific characteristic, it is called a "real existent characteristic" (*dravyasat-lakṣaṇa*).
Subsequently, when the seeking mind again takes blue and so forth as its object, it does not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue as being the specific characteristic;
therefore, it is said that "resembling" means superimposing a characteristic that is not actually existent. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
Some explain that when one seeks out the mind and so forth,
taking what lacks its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) to be its own specific characteristic, this is called "superimposition" (samāropa);
this is not a common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Because one seeks that which is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), we now say it is not so.
If the object of focus (*ālambana*) sought by the mind were not shared [with others],
there would have to be a third characteristic apart from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the third characteristic, what is it that is not subsumed under the non-common?
Furthermore, is the mind of investigation a conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*)?
If it is a conventional cognition, [then...]
Preface: Conventional cognition and its designations function solely in reliance upon the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
if they were not common characteristics, they would contradict the claim that they are merely conventional expressions.
Furthermore, it is also admitted that seeking occurs within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
How could this not be a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)? [Objection: Both conceptual cognition (*kalpanā*) and its verbal expression do not possess the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
they function based on a semblance of a real entity.
The object-like appearance is not real;
it is like a mere conventional phenomenon that does not exist.

How, then, could there be seeds perfumed by names and expressions that signify meaning? Answer: If that underlying essence (*bimba*) were a phenomenon capable of being produced, [then such seeds would exist].
The image-part (nimitta-bhāga) resembles that [object].
By the power of this mental engagement with names and words,
it causes this image-part to be perfumed so as to form its seeds.
Since the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is not provisional, there is likewise no fault.
The treatise states: "The transformative [consciousness] is twofold, namely cause and fruit."
There are many interpretations;
however, according to the meaning of the treatise and this primary commentary,
the transformation of the cause consists solely of the seeds.
The transformation of the fruit consists solely of the active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Even if the present moment were to infuse a seed, it would not be called the "transformation of the cause. Why is this?

The treatise states only that "one cause is capable of transformation," namely, the two types of causal latencies within the eighth consciousness: those of uniform outflow (*nisyanda*) and those of maturation (*vipāka*).
Since it specifies that these are the two types of causal latencies within the eighth consciousness, [it follows that they are not the seeds of other consciousnesses].
The seven manifest perfumers do not exist within the eighth consciousness,
nor are they latencies;
they are not identical to the three characteristics.
The various texts concerning the three characteristics (trilakṣaṇa) do not speak with uniformity;

furthermore, there is no distinct textual passage that speaks of two types of transformation (pariṇāma). If this is so, under which transformation is the perfuming of seeds by the manifest (vartamāna) subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed under the transformation of the fruit (phala-pariṇāma).
Or perhaps it is not both transformed.
Why? Because if one says that the cause is not habitual tendencies (vāsanā).

If it is argued that the five and seven fruits cannot manifest the characteristics of those seeds, [we reply: Question: If that were so, would the meaning of being subsumed under the two transformations not be incomplete? Answer: What fault is there in its being incomplete?
For the two transformations are established based on what is predominant.
However, regarding the enumeration of categories in the *Śūyao*, they are explained according to their meaning:
either the manifest [phenomena] and the seeds are both "capable transformers" (*nengbian*),
or if they are described as "fruits" (*guo*).
How could that which is perfumed by the five [consciousnesses] and the seventh [manas] be a manifest appearance?

The meaning here is that what is manifested by self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) is designated as "various appearances. If this is so, why is it not said that the perfuming agents are also causes for transformation? The answer is: according to the eighth [consciousness] discussed below, manifest appearances are also called seeds.
However, it is said that while the latencies (vāsanā) are predominant and manifest as a continuous stream,
the manifest causes are interrupted and thus omitted from the discussion.
Treatise.

In this context, for now, it is said that "the ālayavijñāna" refers to that which is clung to as "I" (*ātma-grāha*). Ximing [Master] interprets this as distinguishing it from the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) that is being projected and fulfilled;
this does not differ from the original commentary. There is also an interpretation that distinguishes it separately.
That which is cherished and stored by me is designated as the *ālaya*;
that which maintains the seeds of defilement is designated as the *ādāna*.
The first transformation, the consciousness that is the fruit of maturation, is called "maturation" (*vipāka*). Now, [the opponent] says: "This is not so."
The *Dana* (Treasury) states that it is not because it maintains defilement that it is called "transformation"; the *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) says:
"It refers to that which undergoes transformation as the basis for the self and phenomena."

Within these two stages, the six consciousnesses are specifically distinguished up to the seventh stage to reveal that the locus of true grasping as a self (ālaya) exists within the state of ego-clinging;
from the eighth stage upward—excluding the stage of the diamond-like samādhi—it does not.
Since the state of manifesting the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) that maintains the seeds of defilement belongs exclusively to the eighth consciousness,
the verse specifically mentions the eighth, the *vipāka* [consciousness].
Now, I say this is not so.
If it were based on the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*),
then the first transformation would not be the very first to be abandoned,
as this would contradict the subsequent passage.
Now, the commentary on this text contains two types of distinctions.
The first is the exclusion of others;
that is to say, the other six consciousnesses are not the true *vipāka* (maturation).
Second, it excludes the self:
although from the eighth stage onward there is true maturation,
it is not the locus of constant attachment through self-grasping.
Because the grasping at a self has already been abandoned, the subsequent commentary states:
"The first transforming consciousness is called the *ālaya* in the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. It further says:
Although this consciousness has many states within its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa),
the fault is most serious at the initial stage of "storing" (ālaya); therefore, it is specifically so designated.
If one takes the dharmas grasped by maturation as the basis for attachment and subsumes these resultant characteristics as its own characteristic,
how could it incur the grave fault of being the first [of the three] ālayas?
Furthermore, the following section distinguishes [the ālayavijñāna] from its relinquishment. Since the prior ālayavijñāna was not the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
this present passage clearly differentiates it from both self and other.
However, that which serves as the basis for the grasping of a self,
which maintains the seeds of defilement and is the resultant consciousness (vipākaphala-vijñāna),
is termed the "transforming" [consciousness].
Because this does not exhaustively encompass all [aspects], it is said "to speak briefly.
The verses may be divided into eleven sections,
because it is unknowable that this consciousness alone exists.
Because they are absent in other consciousnesses, they are treated as separate categories.
Because they are distinct from and dissociated from feeling (*vedanā*), there are eleven [categories].
Alternatively, if feeling is subsumed within the category of mental factors (*caitta*), there are ten categories.
If it were unknowable, then the two modes of activity would not be distinguished as separate doors;
since they are explained apart from sensation, there are only ten doors.
Treatise.
Regarding "the capacity to conceal" (*nīvaraṇa*) and "that which is concealed" (*nīvarita*), the Sanming Monastery [commentary] provides three interpretations.
The first is that the eight manifest [consciousnesses] are viewed in relation to the other manifest [consciousnesses].
The second [interpretation] takes the seeds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) as the "concealer" (*ālaya*),
because the seeds are able to sustain their fruits.
The third [interpretation] holds that both the manifest and the seeds are capable of concealing.
The second [interpretation] is accepted; the *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium) likewise accepts the second as correct, stating:

"In relation to the substance of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the seeds of defilement are merely its basis (*āśraya*) and do not possess the sense of being its cause-conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*)."
Because the seven evolving consciousnesses, when compared to the eighth [consciousness], also lack both cause and condition even in their manifestation,
the second explanation is that of this school.
However, among the three characteristics, it is the characteristic of cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*).
This differs slightly from that meaning. Now, it is said that when various treatises speak of the "store" (ālaya) as both subject and object, they do not refer exclusively to seeds (*bīja*).
Furthermore, Asvabhāva states:
"The *ālayavijñāna* is proven to be named *ālaya* [because it is the store of all phenomena]."
That which is able to contain and store all phenomena refers to being "perfumed" (vāsita), which is the meaning of "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā).
Since it is stated that one realizes the ālayavijñāna and names it the "ālaya," [it follows that this is its defining characteristic].
Furthermore, it is stated that what "gathers and stores all phenomena" refers to the perfumed [basis],
which clearly indicates the eighth consciousness,
and not the seeds of all phenomena.
If the seeds of affliction (saṃkleśa) are termed "that which stores" (ālaya),
it is thereby proven that the term "seed" (bīja) refers to the ālayavijñāna;
the same would apply to the seeds of the Sautrāntika school.
What does this have to do with the eighth [consciousness]? That treatise further states:
"For this reason, it is again called the 'all-seed consciousness' (sarvabījaka-vijñāna) because it possesses all seeds."
Because they arise and perish simultaneously,
and because the ālayavijñāna and the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) serve as mutual conditions for one another,
they mutually contain and store [each other]. If one speaks of the seeds themselves as the "seed-consciousness" (bījavijñāna), [it refers to this].
How could it be that a seed arises and perishes simultaneously with another seed, such that this is called "mutual containment"?
Furthermore, if Vasubandhu were to explain the first phrase by means of the second phrase...
That which is realized as the seed is called the "capable store" (*nibandhaka*).
For what reason, then, does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* state:
"Furthermore, for what reason is this consciousness called the *ālayavijñāna*?"
This means that all dharmas belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) that have arisen are stored within this [consciousness],
and furthermore, this very consciousness is stored within them.
Since it is said that this consciousness is stored within that [ālayavijñāna],
the seeds must therefore reside in the storehouse of the present life.
If this is the case, then...
Why, then, does it further state that "some sentient beings grasp this consciousness as a self"?
Could one possibly maintain that the seeds and manifestations of the defiled [dharmas] are the self?
Therefore, the term "seed-consciousness" does not refer merely to the seeds.
Because it manifests as the eighth [consciousness] which is capable of encompassing seeds,
it is called the "seed-consciousness.
Therefore, among various designations, it is said that it is "alternatively named the seed-consciousness."
Because it is able to universally sustain all seeds,
Vasubandhu explains the first phrase by means of the second phrase.
Furthermore, Asvabhāva says:
Regarding the term "that which gathers and stores" (*saṃgraha*),
this indicates its capacity to maintain habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
for it is not by the mere presence of habitual tendencies that something is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
It must be able to maintain the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
As it is said regarding the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), this "mind" (*manas*) reveals the eighth consciousness.
It receives the name *ālaya* because it is able to maintain habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because it maintains habitual tendencies,
it is like the sixth consciousness of the Sautrāntika masters.
If one takes the various seeds to be merely habitual tendencies (vāsanā) designated as the *ālayavijñāna*,
then the analogy of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is also not similar; for those [seeds] are potentialities, while that [consciousness] is manifest.
Because there is a distinction; furthermore, this treatise, in its third [chapter], correctly explains that verse as follows:
"Because this fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) possesses all seeds, it is able to store and conceal all defiled phenomena (saṃkleśadharma)."
Based on this, the name *ālaya-vijñāna* is established.

According to this principle, can it be concluded that the name *ālaya* for the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) refers solely to its being the storehouse that contains the resultant phenomena within its seeds? Furthermore, it is said that it is also "appropriated and clung to as a self by sentient beings."
If one speaks of seeds,
