Furthermore, the treatise states that all noble ones feel weary of and detached from that which possesses form, and so forth.
The present commentary relies on explicit statements to indicate that those in the form realm [who attain the fruit of] anāgāmin are shown [to be born in the formless realm]. Ximing states:
"This teaching implies that those such as anāgāmins who loathe the form realm and are born in the formless realm will certainly not be reborn below."
As for the statement that the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is not mentioned:
it is because those with material bodies (*rūpakāya*) go to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Now, we say this is not so, because it contradicts the subsequent passage.
The text below states: "Therefore, those currently residing [here] and those who will be born [here] transform into this realm;
it does not say that those who are to go there transform.
If one were to allow that those going there transform..."
Those in the formless realm also come and stand by the Buddha’s side;
they too must be admitted to undergo transformation.
How much more so for those in the lower realms? Furthermore, this is difficult to refute.
Even if there were material bodies vastly different in scale, such as coarse and subtle,
what use would there be for one transforming into the other? Therefore,
the original interpretation is correct.
Treatise:
Therefore, when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed or when it is first being formed, it likewise manifests transformation.
Question: When it is about to be formed, can beings from other realms be used [to populate it]?
When there is transformation and decay, for what purpose does another transformation arise?
Since another transformation arises,
the cause of that transformation must exist.
When will there be an end? Answer: It changes because the karma that brings about other births within this realm matures.
If it were not so, then since the duration of its abiding is the same as this change, why would this realm not be destroyed as soon as it arises?
From this, one knows that the transformation of the *āśraya* (basis) occurs through the karma of others;
for example, in this life, the transformation of the basis of another causes its dissolution and rebirth in another realm,
or the transformation of the basis of another causes it to enter parinirvāṇa.
There are those that become bloated and gradually rot and decay;
when the power of the karma that caused their destruction is exhausted, the three calamities also cease.
Furthermore, it is by virtue of this that the realm originally transformed from its source acts as the drawing cause.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that the three lower meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are spoken of in terms of internal defects based on their projecting causes;
this is because the karma coexistent with those [defects] brings about the formation of those respective realms.
The calamities that arise at other times are drawn forth by those [primary ones].
Otherwise, what would be the purpose of the statement "the others are drawn forth by these"?
Therefore, this is not a secondary explanatory method (anuvartana-mukha), but is based on the actual reality.
When the momentum of the projecting cause is exhausted, all these things are extinguished. Question:
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states that sometimes the end of a kalpa is manifested, burning heaven and earth until they are all ablaze;
yet sentient beings harbor the notion of permanence.
It is illuminated so that they may know it ceases quickly;
this is produced through the transformative power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Why, then, would it not [benefit] sentient beings? Answer: Transformation does not obstruct [the process], but it is simply not a real destruction.
Actual destruction results from karma, not from the power of supernormal faculties;
for if it were determined by supernatural power,
the timing of the destruction would be indefinite.
Therefore, the previous objection stated:
"It must truly transform into this defiled land. If one were to grant that the world is truly transformed and destroyed by calamities, [then the following would follow].
There is the fallacy of contradiction.
In this present passage,
it is stated that actual formation and destruction occur.
Not relying on the doctrine of transformation, one asks: at the time of the destruction of a kalpa, does that matter of the empty realm (ākāśadhātu-rūpa) exist or not?
If it exists, what is it that is not destroyed?
If it does not exist, this contradicts the sūtras.
The Sūtra states: "In the empty kalpa, there is only the manifestation of color in the form of cavities;
this is the color of the space-element (ākāśa-dhātu). Answer: Although it exists, it is not subject to destruction.
This is because it is not produced by the karma of formation or destruction.
If it is granted that because they are functional, others are both permanent and subject to change,
then the three calamities would also be functional,
and others would likewise be both permanent and subject to change.
If [the transformation] were included within formation and destruction, it would follow that there must be formation and destruction;

for this reason, we know that although it is a transformation produced by the consciousness of another, it is not included within formation and destruction. Question: Even if one grants that there is a transformation in another realm or one's own stage when [a being] is born there, [is this still not included?]
Just as with the waters of the great ocean in this world-system,
do sentient beings of the desire realm undergo transformation in the same way?
If it is granted that they do transform in the same way, [then...]
The gods of the desire realm ought to see the lower waters as lapis lazuli.
Since they see it as lapis lazuli, their perception does not undergo transformation.
Even if their perception does not transform, do the gods still have water? Answer: The treatises state that because they share [the object] in common, it can indeed be transformed together.
The ocean is not shared;
it does not change its water.
If that were so, then [the water] in the eight hot great hells and other such places would not be used by the noble ones (*ārya*).
[Objection: It should not transform that [earth]. [Response: Because it appears as being of the same level. [Objection: If that were so, water and the like should likewise [transform].
[Response: For the gods, it appears as being of the same level. [Objection: The great ocean transforms uniformly. [Response:
Those who see it as lapis lazuli speak of it as distinct water. [Objection: If that were so, fish and other creatures dwelling in the water would immediately see it as houses.
Sentient beings within the great ocean should likewise see houses;
if it is granted that they do not see the ocean, [then this principle holds].
This would not be a transformation within the same level (*bhūmi*).
If it were admitted that one sees the seawater and so forth, then one should not construct dwellings [there]. Answer: It is admitted that there are separate dwellings situated upon the seawater.
Just as they dwell in burrows in the earth due to the distinctions of their karmic power,
so too do other distinct waters exist in a single location with four boundaries.
In principle, this is not precluded,
due to the influence of individual karma,
as in the case of solitary prisons and the like.
Regarding the phrase "the power of meditative concentration,
supernormal powers, and so forth," Ximing states that "and so forth" includes the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The *Chuan-sanzang* (Record of the Tripitaka Master) also states that the power of vows is equal [to the other powers]. Some say that "equal" includes ten types of transformative powers (*nirmāṇa*), and that concentration (*samādhi*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and vows are the same as the four [powers].
It is said that the Buddha’s power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is also equal. Now, I say this is not so.
If it is through the Buddha’s empowerment, it is subsumed under the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
The upholding of the sūtra and divine mantras is subsumed under the power of the Dharma.
The powers of various transformations, the power of afflictions (*kleśa*), and the power of transforming precious jewels and pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) are likewise included.
This is subsumed under the power of prior karma. The *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium) states:
"The eighth [category] is transformation by the three powers;
as for the Buddhas and others providing empowerment, it is no different from granting a vow. This is also not the case.
This supernormal power is due to empowerment;
it is not the result of the power of aspiration.
Treatise.
And it includes actual matter (rūpa) subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Ximing’s commentary explains:
"The eighth [consciousness] takes the real as its object, not the conventional."
However, the previous explanation regarding the "middle position" already admits that the eighth consciousness also takes conceptual (prajñapti) form as its object;
this is judged to be the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla. Thus it is said:
The eighth [consciousness] does not take as its object the hidden [aspects] such as birth and so forth;
it takes as its object the manifest [aspects] such as long and short.

Furthermore, by citing the *ādarśajñāna* (mirror-like wisdom) which takes the eighteen [realms] in their full perfection as its object, it is proven that the eighth [consciousness] takes the conventional (*prajñapti*) as its object. If this is the case, then within the present *dharmāyatana* (sphere of mental objects), it should likewise take the conventional as its object.
How could it be that they take only the real?
Therefore, the original commentary judges that taking only the real as the object of cognition is the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla.
If the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) takes as its object [forms] such as square or round and realizes them as being conventionally designated based on eight conditions,
it should likewise take as its objects conventional characteristics such as the past, the future, arising, and abiding,
because the mirror-like wisdom takes them as its objects.
Therefore, cause and effect are distinct and cannot be analogized to one another. Furthermore, it is said:
"The matter produced by the dhyānas of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) also possesses practical utility;
that which is called 'majestic power' (vaibhūtika) refers to the fundamental dhyānas."
The "Vajra-like Samādhi" (Vijaya-nāma-vīrya-samādhi) is not [the one referred to here];

we maintain that this is not so. If it were granted that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) could transform actual matter (*rūpa*) through meditative concentration, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter thirteen, state:
This refers to transcending the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
whereby transformation possesses actual efficacy.
If it is said that their teaching encompasses both [transformation and] pervasion, [it is so].
This statement regarding those who undergo transformation through meditative concentration is also not correct.
Even with the power of supernormal abilities (*ṛddhi-bala*), which is superior, one must still transcend the second eon before such transformation becomes functional.
The power of concentration is inferior.
How could it be granted that an ordinary transformation possesses practical efficacy?
Therefore, majestic concentration is produced by superior persons.
[The *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya*] states in the thirty-third [verse]: "Because non-noble supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are unfit for use. Question:
Since transformations are permitted, how many atoms (*paramāṇu*) are transformed in each of the upper and lower realms?
The Ximing commentary says:
Through the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), one relies upon the retributive essence (*vipākadhātu*) of the desire and form realms to produce transformations.
In the desire realm, all five [objects] are present;
in the higher realms, odor and taste are excluded. Now, it is said:
The fragrance above also transforms.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Even unto the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*), by smelling the fragrance, one knows where [the Buddha] resides."
If it is said that those [objects] were previously categorized under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and are now being discussed as the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*),
why are they specifically and invariably transformed into these five objects?
They ought all to remain within the sphere of phenomena.

If, despite being produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth, it is not included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), then what is it that is so included? If one were to say:
"Even though it is transformed by the eighth [consciousness] through the striking force of meditative concentration and so forth..."

Because these are material forms that are the fruits of karma, they constitute the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). If those which are the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth were instead material forms belonging to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*),
then the Buddha would possess only the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Since it is accepted that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) necessarily arise together with the five formless elements (*ārūpya-dhātu*) and so forth, we know that in the higher realms, the objects of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*) also undergo transformation. [The Ximing Commentary] asks: The five sense organs (*indriya*) and the five sense objects (*viṣaya*) abide in the same location as appropriate for each.
Are they produced by four distinct sets of the four great elements,
or are they produced by a single set of the four great elements? If they were produced by a single set of the four great elements, [then...]
What is the yoga? At the stage of the *kalala*,
are the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), etc.,
produced simultaneously by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), or are they produced sequentially?
If they were produced by separate primary elements (*mahābhūta*), why does [the *Pañcavastuka*] state that only seven things share the same location as the eye?
That text asks: "Within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), how many things are included within the eye?"
Answer: If categorized according to their distinct characteristics,
there is only one thing,
namely, the pure matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
If categorized according to inseparable inclusion,
there are seven substances:
namely, the eye, the body, earth, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
The Tripitaka Master’s commentary states:
"Being in the same location" means that there is only one primary great element (*mahābhūta*).
When one infers this through reasoning, it is because the five sense organs and their physical bases occupy the same location.
The great elements of the first stage constitute the formative basis; as for what is said regarding the formation of the four great elements of the eye,
it follows the nature of the formed phenomena.
They are designated as the great element of the eye-organ,
and so on, up to the great element of the tangible that acts as the creator;
in reality, however, they are a single great element.
This explains that the seven substances exist;

they exist simultaneously, and because the initial [moment] possesses the capacity to produce the eye and so forth, they are said to be "co-existent" (*sahabhū*). Question: Why is it that fire and so forth do not exist [in this way]?
"Vitality, heat, and consciousness—these three are never dissociated from one another, except in the formless realm. The commentary explains:
although fire and so forth actually exist [in those realms], the fifty-four [types of beings] speak only of seven substances.
According to the explicit explanation of the characteristics,
because the nature of solidity of the earth serves as the basis for the eyes and so forth,
it is specifically mentioned.

The treatise distinguishes two types of transformation based on causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*): the first is the transformation of the two [consciousnesses], and the second is the transformation of the eighth mind-king alone as a causal condition. Regarding the second, it is held that only the eighth consciousness, the mind-king, undergoes transformation as a causal condition.
What is meant by "having practical utility"?
There are two kinds of practical utility.
For example, the quality of resistance is the practical utility of matter (*rūpa*).
Second, regarding the nature of the objective basis:
if that is so, why is that which is transformed by the five consciousnesses not the objective basis for the sixth consciousness?
Why is it not its causal condition?
If it is argued that because the function of non-obstruction lacks these two meanings,
the length and so forth transformed by the eighth consciousness would also merely serve as the primary object (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and should not be considered causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*),
the Dharma Master himself has stated:

If that is so, the first interpretation is superior. Question: Since the eighth [consciousness] resides in the mind-element (*manodhātu*), its object of perception (*ālambana*) should be exclusively the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
How, then, is it compatible with the eighteen elements? Answer: It depends on those six pairs of objects.
The mind-base (manāyatana) is subsumed within the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) as its object;
it does not depend on the six pairs of objects.
According to those respective objects, it is subsumed within the eighteen [elements].

Furthermore, since darkness is subsumed under light within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), why are they not established as separate bases (*āyatana*) and elements? Answer: Because of the meanings of base, element, production, and cause.
The mental base (*manāyatana*) is subsumed within the object-base (*dharmāyatana*), because the eighth [consciousness] has no separate arising as its cause;
it is also included within the six mental bases. Question: If the transformed image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the five consciousnesses is unobstructed, [how is this so]?
This contradicts the third characteristic of the Abhidharma.
In that treatise, within the analysis of the resistant (*sapratigha*) and non-resistant (*apratigha*), it states:
"All things that are visible (*sanidarśana*) are necessarily resistant."
Is it not the case that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of visual consciousness lacks visibility?
That treatise states:
"The meaning of 'having visibility' refers to the objective sphere traversed by the eye."
Therefore, that which is associated with visual consciousness is called "possessing vision.
If one speaks of it as "possessing resistance," this refers to resistance regarding its objective sphere (*ālambana-pratighāta*).
The principle that "non-obstructive resistance" is also untenable;
for they claim it is called "resistance" because of three causes.
That is to say: by way of their genus,
by way of their accumulation,
and by way of their lack of cultivation.
"Kind" (jāti) refers to that which acts as a mutual obstruction between one thing and another;
"accumulation" (saṃcita) refers to that which consists of more than a single atom (paramāṇu), because a single atom lacks resistance.
That which is not cultivated or refined is not a form that arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Here, there are two interpretations.
One says that all forms transformed by the five consciousnesses possess resistance;
thus, it speaks of "having visibility" (*sanidarśana*) as a general example to illustrate the rest.
That is, according to the Abhidharma,
those that have visibility are called "with resistance" (*sapratigha*); one [school] says they are "without resistance," because they do not possess visibility.
The objective domain traversed by the eye is called "visible.

This is because the eye faculty merely illuminates its essential nature (*svabhāva*). If that is so, why is it called the "faculty that shares the same object"? The answer is: because they apprehend the same essential nature together.
As it is said: "That which is shared by a king has a single object of cognition (ālambana), or there are three types of resistance (sapratigha).
The substance (dravya) possesses all three;
the aspect (ākāra) possesses only the latter two."
The general term is "with resistance" (sapratigha).
"Resistance" (pratigha) does not mean mere obstruction;
here, it refers specifically to the resistance of having a material substance as its transformed object.
This is called "practical utility. The characteristics of the five consciousnesses do not exist [independently].

It might be argued that the seven consciousnesses should be subsumed under "discriminative transformation" (vikalpa-pariṇāma) merely because they take objects as their domain; however, this is not the case,
for since they arise from sovereign meditative concentration (vaśitā-samādhi), they possess actual functional efficacy.
Why is it not a causal condition (*pratyaya*)? Answer: Because of the distinction between the concentrated (*samāhita*) and the non-concentrated (*asamāhita*).
That which is produced by mastery (*vaśitā*) serves as food and so forth;
thus, it cannot be treated as an analogy. If that is so, then the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) would also be transformations of causal conditions.
Because there is edible food, this [explanation] may be acceptable; however, another interpretation is also incorrect.
Being for the consumption of others constitutes the causal condition (*pratyaya*), whereas the fivefold transformation for one's own use does not constitute a causal condition.
